newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Local polls could affect NATO Bosnia withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Local polls could affect NATO Bosnia withdrawal.

text.p: Any further delay in Bosnian municipal elections scheduled for late November could affect the planned December withdrawal of NATO-led peace forces from the country, a NATO spokesman implied on Wednesday.

The spokesman, Major Brett Boudreau, said municipal voting would place an even greater demand on NATO troops than September 14 national and regional polls which saw virtually the entire force involved in logistics and security support.
"I don't think we could really nail down a precise figure with respect to how much would be required to support the elections," Boudreau told reporters in Sarajevo.
"Certainly for the national elections we said that the majority, some 50,00 plus troops, were engaged one way or the other in support of those elections."

"For the municipals it will be perhaps a little more challenging than the presidential elections in the sense that voting will take place over a three-day period, so that will add a different security dimension to it," he said, adding that the winter weather would present another problem.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is charged with staging elections in Bosnia under a mandate provided by the Dayton peace agreement.
Municipal elections were originally planned to be held along with the September 14 polls, but voter registration irregularities led to them being postponed until late November.

OSCE's independent election monitor on Tuesday urged that the municipal elections be postponed until the spring of 1997, insisting that months of remedial effort are required to create credible voting conditions.
Although NATO's current mandate in Bosnia expires on December 20, 1996, a follow-on force of some significance is expected to be agreed after U.S. elections in early November.
NATO defence ministers meeting in Bergen, Norway, on Wednesday confirmed as much without specifying the size or composition of the force, or its mission.
OSCE could still decide to proceed with Bosnian municipal elections in November, in which case all of NATO's current combat-ready troops would be available for support duty.
But if the municipal vote were postponed until next Spring, as the OSCE's top monitor urged on Tuesday, the new force would have to be big enough to handle election security and logistics.

The general assumption is that policing municipal polls will be even more difficult and demanding than national ones, especially if large numbers of refugees try to cross de facto ethnic boundaries to cast votes, as is expected.
Boudreau said NATO was still working on the assumption of a November date for municipal elections.
"We're not really looking at any contingencies for a spring election," he said.
